extracted.intended_audience: insurance practitioners / actuaries and educated general readers interested in physical education and hygienic therapeutics
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and compute net, equal annual, and single life-insurance premiums and policy reserves using mortality tables and a chosen interest rate; includes explanatory examples and worked calculations. (The page also presents hygienic/physical-education treatment guidelines for various diseases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rickets — dietary and physical treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best physic for a rickety child is milk, bran-bread, and fruit; the best physician, the drill-master of the turner-hall."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books should be thrown aside until the child's back is straightened; knock-knees, bow-legs, 'chicken-breasts,' and round shoulders are amenable to treatment if begun in time — during the first three years of the teens (most plastic period).

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral cure for young topers, smokers, and gluttons
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishments are only of temporary avail and homilies of no use; the success depends upon "silencing the tempter — by outbidding his offer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide healthful diversions (sports, hunting expeditions, mountain-excursions, or Olympic games). Between exciting diversions and sound sleep the toper will forget his tipple; relieve the reaction by diverting sports to reduce relapse risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection and rehabilitation for children of inebriates
rubrics_metrics.description: Children of confirmed inebriates should be carefully guarded against objective temptations and the promptings of a peculiar disposition (periodical apathy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Healthful amusements and healthy food rarely fail to restore mental tone; even before puberty, manifestations of a more buoyant temper will show recovery from hereditary hebetude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chlorosis (green-sickness) — recommended hygienic cure
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best cure is a mountain-excursion, afoot or on horseback; the next best a course of 'calisthenics,' a plentiful and varying vegetable diet, fun, frequent baths, and plenty of sleep."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'tonic' drugs (they aggravate the evil). Note: stimulants like strong green tea may momentarily relieve but produce a worse reaction afterward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mistaking stimulants for cures
rubrics_metrics.description: Tonic medicines and temporary stimulants produce morbid and transient stimulation which is commonly mistaken for permanent invigoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that transient relief (from stimulants or teas) may increase later nervous depression and impede true reconstruction/recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulmonary consumption (early tuberculosis) — diagnosis and outdoor cure
rubrics_metrics.description: In early stages pulmonary consumption is perhaps the most curable of chronic diseases; impure air is the original cause and out-door life the only radical cure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize early symptoms (hoarseness, dry rasping cough, rapid pulse, general lassitude; spitting blood and chest pains more characteristic). Use exertion (walking upstairs, uphill) to test respiratory acceleration. Treatment: remove bedroom windows, keep patient in open air (walking, riding, or sitting), provide adequate clothing, increase exercise (running, walking, chest-expanding gymnastics) while ensuring outdoor activity is made pleasant enough to be permanent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise must be durable and pleasurable to be effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine-exercises often are discontinued once they relieve momentary distress; the problem is to make outdoor exercise pleasant enough to be permanently preferable to an indolent life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer varied, enjoyable outdoor occupations and pursuits (e.g., gardening, well-digging, supervised constructive labor) that keep patients active long-term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherited tubercular diathesis is not insuperable — tailor rehabilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A tubercular diathesis inherited from both parents need not prevent successful cure; purposeful out-door work can restore health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match treatment to patient's character/interests (case example: horticultural and constructive outdoor tasks cured a consumptive youth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic philosophy: prefer hygienic (non-medicinal) treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: With few exceptions, internal use of drugs will be discarded by intelligent physicians; disease is a restorative operation and should be treated by conformity to natural laws rather than poison-drugs or supernatural remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize fresh air, natural diet, exercise, sleep, baths, and other hygienic measures over drug-based tonics and nostrums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural instincts and free inquiry as guides to health
rubrics_metrics.description: Healthy nations preserve health by following palatable food and natural inclinations; anti-natural doctrines (confinement, distrust of fresh air, toxic remedies) are injurious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust sensory intuition for selecting food and environment; oppose medical or moral doctrines that require unnatural treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental difference: life vs property insurance (premium design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazard attaching to buildings or ships may remain unchanged and premiums for such property can be fixed annually; the same methods cannot be applied to human life because mortality increases with age and health can change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt one uniform periodic premium for the whole term of proposed life insurance rather than annual renewal with re-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of net premium
rubrics_metrics.description: "By net premium is meant the amount calculated from a certain mortality table, and rate of interest, without any addition for expenses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute net premium strictly from mortality and interest assumptions; expense loadings are excluded at this stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of actuarial standard assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The article employs the American Experience Table and 4½ per cent interest as the official standard for the State of New York.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a mortality table and interest rate as the basis for premium and reserve calculations; results depend on those choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal annual premium (level annual premium) computation method
rubrics_metrics.description: Method: consider the number living at each age and the number of deaths; if equal payments are collected from survivors at the beginning of each year and $1 is paid at each death, calculate the requisite annual premium by equating total contributions to death-claims over the period (example produced premium $0.52027).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count total contributions (number_living × payments over years) and total death-claims, then compute the payment per person that funds the expected claims (before discounting for interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include interest by discounting contributions and claims (present value method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Premiums are payable at the beginning while death-claims are due at the end of the year; bring amounts to a common basis by computing the present value of each sum at the chosen interest rate (example uses present-value factors $0.9569, $0.9157, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply each contribution and each death-claim by the appropriate present-value factor for its timing; solve for the premium that makes present value of contributions equal present value of claims (example reduces premium from $0.52027 to $0.49432).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single premium (single-payment for life) calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The single premium for life equals the present value of all future death-claims divided by the number of persons to provide for them (example: present value of future death-claims $779.10 ÷ 847 persons = $0.91987).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute PV of future liabilities at start age, divide by number of insured lives to get the one-time premium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve / net valuation for policies
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of each year an unexpended balance remains; dividing this balance by the number of survivors gives the amount that applies to each individual living at that period — called the net valuation or reserve for each policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute annual fund balance after paying death-claims and accruing interest; reserve per policy = balance ÷ number living at period end (worked example provides reserves at successive ages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Premium composition: insurance cost + reserve fund
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual premium may be looked upon as consisting of two parts: one defraying the annual cost of insurance dependent upon the death-rate, the other put aside as a reserve fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing premiums, separate the component that covers immediate expected deaths from that which accumulates to meet future liabilities (reserves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of payments matters: premiums in advance vs claims at year-end
rubrics_metrics.description: Premiums are payable at the beginning, while death-claims are due at the end of the same year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This timing difference requires appropriate present-value adjustments (discounting premiums or discounting claims) when computing net premiums and reserves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical variation: reserve calculation methods differ
rubrics_metrics.description: While the reserve, as here given, is strictly correct for the example, other methods of calculation are employed in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware actuaries may use alternative valuation methods; the explanatory method provided serves as a simple foundation rather than the only practical algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of age-specific death-rates to compute cost and reserve
rubrics_metrics.description: Given death-rates per cent by age, compute the cost of insurance for that year and the reserve applicable to each age (table demonstrates death-rate, cost of insurance, and reserve columns for ages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply mortality percentages for each year of age to determine annual insurance cost; track reserve accumulation and changes across years to inform premium structure.
